survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD PISA 2012 framework describes the assessment design (rotated test booklets, background questionnaires, and optional computer-based mathematics) rather than reporting an empirical ML model with a specific analytic dataset. PISA is implemented as a complex, multi-stage survey of 15-year-olds sampled within countries and schools, with rotated booklet designs that require survey-aware estimation when producing population-representative results. The framework does not specify particular weight variables (e.g., student sampling weights or replicate weights) for analysts, so the exact weight variable names cannot be extracted from the provided text. For any downstream empirical analysis using PISA microdata, analysts should apply the official PISA student sampling weights and replicate weights provided in the dataset documentation to account for unequal selection probabilities and the complex design; if weights are omitted, results may be biased and standard errors may be misestimated.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This document is an assessment and analytical framework describing how PISA 2012 mathematics is constructed, administered, and reported, not an empirical study that estimates student achievement using plausible values (PV) or reports a missing-data strategy. Because no student-level achievement modeling results are presented here, PV handling and missing-data handling are not part of the reported methodology in this text. Any PV and missing-data procedures would be specified in the separate PISA technical documentation and analysis manuals rather than in this framework chapter.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The text specifies that PISA 2012 targets 15-year-old students enrolled in school-based and work-based educational programmes, with typical country samples of between 4,500 and 10,000 students from at least 150 schools. It also describes rotated test designs where different students receive different combinations of test clusters, and that students complete a background questionnaire (about 30 minutes) and school principals complete a questionnaire (about 20 minutes), with additional optional questionnaires in some countries. For the illustrative item analyses, a constraint is stated that standards were analysed for two sets of countries: nine OECD countries (Australia [New South Wales], Flemish Belgium, Canada [Alberta], Finland, Ireland, Japan, Korea, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom) and six high-performing countries (Flemish Belgium, Canada [Alberta], Chinese Taipei, Finland, Korea, and Singapore), with the additional constraint that standards had to be available in English.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD framework explains the theoretical and operational basis of PISA 2012 mathematics assessment, where mathematical literacy is defined as the capacity to formulate, employ, and interpret mathematics in a variety of contexts. The mathematics domain is organized by three processes (formulating, employing, interpreting/evaluating), four content categories (quantity; space and shape; change and relationships; uncertainty and data), and four context categories (personal, occupational, societal, scientific), with target score-point distributions of about 25/50/25 across processes and about 25/25/25/25 across content and context categories. The assessment uses paper-and-pencil tests with rotated booklet designs (four 30-minute clusters per student for the core paper-based assessment) and includes an optional computer-based mathematics component (40 minutes total, four 20-minute clusters across rotated forms). Results are reported on scales with an average of 500 and standard deviation of 100, and proficiency levels are described for mathematics (including process and content subscales). The document also details item formats, scoring (including partial credit for some constructed responses), and the role of calculators and digital tools, but it does not provide empirical predictive model performance.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is a non-empirical assessment framework rather than an empirical ML paper: it does not estimate a predictive model, report PV-based achievement outcomes, or provide country-level analytic sample sizes. Consequently, fields such as total_students, per-country n_students, PV handling, missing-data handling, and ML techniques are not applicable to the framework’s purpose. The sparse extraction of countries reflects only those explicitly named in the illustrative standards-analysis constraint, not the full set of 66 participating PISA 2012 countries/economies.
